Presented are novel systems and techniques for an electric vehicle (EV) powertrain that includes a continuously variable transmission (CVT) connected to an electric drive motor. A control system is arranged to regulate the CVT and/or the drive motor in order to improve different efficiency measures relating to the EV and its components.

The control system may be set up to run the EV in an economy mode. In that mode, it coordinates operation of both the CVT and the drive motor at the same time to maximize the vehicle’s driving range. The system may control the amount of current delivered to the drive motor while also changing the CVT’s transmission speed ratio.

The disclosed system is an electric vehicle powertrain that combines an electric drive motor with a continuously variable transmission (CVT). By integrating a CVT into the electric powertrain, the system allows the relationship between motor speed and vehicle speed to be varied continuously, rather than being limited to fixed gear ratios. This enables the drive motor to operate more often within efficient speed and torque regions while still delivering the desired vehicle performance.

A control system is provided to manage operation of both the CVT and the electric drive motor. The control system coordinates these components to improve overall vehicle efficiency as well as the efficiency of individual subsystems, such as the motor, transmission, and battery. Rather than controlling the motor and transmission independently, the system may evaluate operating conditions and command both the motor output and the CVT speed ratio in a coordinated manner.

In an economy operating mode, the control system simultaneously controls the CVT and the drive motor to optimize the driving range of the electric vehicle. For example, the controller may select a transmission speed ratio that permits the motor to run at a more efficient operating point while also limiting or regulating the electrical energy consumed by the motor. This coordinated control can reduce losses, improve energy utilization, and extend the distance the vehicle can travel on a given battery charge.

The control system may regulate the current or power supplied to the electric drive motor while also adjusting the CVT transmission speed ratio. In some operating conditions, the controller may reduce motor current demand and compensate by modifying the CVT ratio to maintain acceptable vehicle acceleration or cruising performance. In other conditions, the controller may adjust the CVT ratio to reduce motor load, thereby lowering power consumption and improving efficiency.

The control strategy may take into account a variety of operating parameters, including battery voltage, throttle position, and the current transmission speed ratio. Battery voltage can be used to assess available electrical energy or power capability, throttle position can indicate driver demand, and transmission speed ratio can indicate the current mechanical relationship between the motor and the driven wheels. By processing these and other inputs, the control system can determine appropriate commands for the motor and the CVT to balance performance, efficiency, and range.

Electric vehicle powertrain systems can be designed to combine an electric drive motor with a continuously variable transmission (CVT) in order to improve overall vehicle efficiency and performance. In such a system, the electric motor supplies driving torque to the wheels through the CVT, while an electronic control system monitors and regulates both the motor and the transmission. Instead of operating the motor and transmission independently, the controller coordinates their behavior so that the vehicle can deliver the required driving power while using electrical energy as efficiently as possible.

The control system receives information from several vehicle operating inputs and sensors. These may include battery voltage, motor current, throttle or accelerator position, vehicle speed, motor speed, and the current speed ratio of the CVT. Based on these inputs, the controller determines how much current or power should be supplied to the electric motor and what transmission ratio should be selected by the CVT. By continuously adjusting these variables, the system can keep the motor operating closer to its most efficient range while still providing the torque and speed demanded by the driver.

A major feature of the system is an economy mode. When economy mode is selected, the controller limits or modifies motor power delivery and simultaneously adjusts the CVT ratio to reduce unnecessary energy consumption. For example, during light acceleration or steady cruising, the controller may reduce motor current while selecting a transmission ratio that allows the motor to run at a more efficient speed. If more power is needed, such as during acceleration or hill climbing, the controller can adjust the ratio and increase motor output in a controlled manner without wasting excess energy.

By coordinating motor operation and transmission ratio in this way, the vehicle can achieve better energy efficiency than it would with a less integrated drivetrain control strategy. The CVT allows the motor to avoid inefficient operating regions, while the motor control system prevents excessive current draw from the battery. Together, these functions reduce energy losses, improve drivability, and help extend the vehicle’s driving range. The key result is a powertrain control approach in which the electric motor and continuously variable transmission are optimized together, especially in economy mode, to make the electric vehicle more efficient and practical for everyday use.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate patent application language for an EV drivetrain control system that manages motor current and CVT ratio based on battery voltage, throttle position, and transmission speed ratio.
counterfactuals.output:
Below is sample patent application language for an electric vehicle drivetrain control system. This is technical drafting language and should be reviewed by a qualified patent professional before filing.

---

## Title

**Electric Vehicle Drivetrain Control System for Coordinated Motor Current and Continuously Variable Transmission Ratio Management**

---

## Abstract

An electric vehicle drivetrain control system includes a traction motor, a battery pack, a continuously variable transmission, and a controller configured to regulate motor current and transmission ratio based on battery voltage, throttle position, and a transmission speed ratio. The controller determines a requested drive output from throttle position, determines an available electrical output based at least in part on battery voltage, and commands a motor current limit and a continuously variable transmission ratio to provide vehicle propulsion while maintaining the battery voltage within a desired operating range. In some embodiments, the controller reduces commanded motor current and adjusts the continuously variable transmission ratio when battery voltage falls below a threshold, thereby improving drivability, battery protection, and drivetrain efficiency.

---

## Field

The present disclosure relates generally to electric vehicle drivetrain control systems and, more particularly, to systems and methods for controlling motor current and a continuously variable transmission ratio in an electric vehicle based on battery voltage, throttle position, and transmission speed ratio.

---

## Background

Electric vehicles commonly employ an electric traction motor powered by a battery pack. Vehicle acceleration and torque output are typically controlled by varying motor current in response to a driver input, such as accelerator pedal or throttle position. In certain vehicle architectures, a continuously variable transmission, or CVT, is provided between the traction motor and one or more driven wheels to vary an effective speed ratio between the motor and the vehicle wheels.

Battery voltage may vary substantially during operation due to state of charge, load, temperature, internal resistance, and transient current demand. When high motor current is commanded while battery voltage is low, vehicle performance may degrade and the battery may be subjected to undesirable stress. Additionally, in a drivetrain having a CVT, transmission ratio selection affects motor operating speed, motor current demand, wheel torque, and system efficiency.

Accordingly, there is a need for an improved drivetrain control system that coordinates motor current control and CVT ratio control based on battery voltage, throttle position, and transmission speed ratio.

---

## Summary

In one embodiment, an electric vehicle drivetrain control system includes a battery pack, an electric traction motor coupled to the battery pack through an inverter, a continuously variable transmission coupled to the traction motor, at least one sensor configured to generate a battery voltage signal, at least one throttle position sensor configured to generate a throttle position signal, and at least one transmission speed sensor configured to generate a transmission speed ratio signal. A controller is configured to receive the battery voltage signal, the throttle position signal, and the transmission speed ratio signal, and to generate a motor current command and a CVT ratio command based on the received signals.

In some embodiments, the controller determines a desired propulsion output based on throttle position and modifies the desired propulsion output based on available battery voltage. The controller may reduce or limit motor current when the battery voltage is below a voltage threshold. The controller may also command a CVT ratio adjustment to maintain the electric traction motor within a target speed or efficiency region while satisfying, to the extent possible, the requested drive output.

In some embodiments, the controller uses the transmission speed ratio to estimate a relationship between motor speed and wheel speed and to determine a current command that provides desired wheel torque without exceeding an electrical limit associated with the battery pack. The controller may further coordinate motor current reduction and CVT ratio change to avoid abrupt changes in vehicle acceleration.

---

## Detailed Description

### System Overview

An electric vehicle drivetrain control system may include a high-voltage battery pack, an inverter or motor drive circuit, an electric traction motor, a continuously variable transmission, and a controller. The electric traction motor may be mechanically coupled to an input of the continuously variable transmission. An output of the continuously variable transmission may be coupled to one or more driven wheels through a differential, axle assembly, chain drive, belt drive, gear reduction, or other torque transfer arrangement.

The battery pack supplies electrical power to the inverter. The inverter controls phase current supplied to the traction motor in response to commands from the controller. The traction motor generates torque that is transmitted through the continuously variable transmission to propel the vehicle.

The continuously variable transmission may include any ratio-varying device capable of changing an effective speed ratio between the motor and the driven wheels. For example, the continuously variable transmission may include a belt-and-pulley CVT, toroidal CVT, traction-drive CVT, hydrostatic CVT, electronically actuated CVT, or other variable ratio transmission. The CVT may include an actuator responsive to a CVT ratio command from the controller.

### Sensors and Inputs

The controller may receive a battery voltage signal representative of voltage of the battery pack. The battery voltage signal may be measured at battery terminals, at an inverter DC bus, or at another electrical node representative of battery voltage.

The controller may also receive a throttle position signal representative of a driver torque request. The throttle position signal may be generated by an accelerator pedal position sensor, hand throttle sensor, twist-grip sensor, lever sensor, drive-by-wire input device, or other operator input device.

The controller may further receive one or more speed signals associated with the continuously variable transmission. In one embodiment, the controller receives a motor speed signal and a transmission output speed signal and determines a transmission speed ratio from the motor speed and the output speed. In another embodiment, the controller receives a direct ratio signal from a CVT position sensor. The transmission speed ratio may correspond to a ratio of motor speed to transmission output speed, a ratio of input pulley speed to output pulley speed, a commanded ratio, an estimated ratio, or another parameter indicative of transmission ratio.

### Control of Motor Current and CVT Ratio

The controller may execute a control routine in which motor current and CVT ratio are jointly determined. The controller may first determine a requested torque, requested power, or requested acceleration based at least in part on throttle position. The controller may then determine an available current or available power based at least in part on battery voltage.

For example, when battery voltage is above a first threshold, the controller may allow a nominal motor current command corresponding to the driver request. When battery voltage falls below the first threshold, the controller may reduce a maximum allowable motor current according to a voltage-dependent derating function. When battery voltage falls below a second lower threshold, the controller may further restrict motor current or enter a protective operating mode.

The controller may determine a desired CVT ratio based on throttle position, battery voltage, transmission speed ratio, motor speed, vehicle speed, motor efficiency, or combinations thereof. In one embodiment, under high throttle demand and adequate battery voltage, the controller commands a ratio that increases wheel torque by allowing the motor to operate near a target speed associated with high torque output. Under low battery voltage, the controller may command a ratio that reduces motor current demand for a given vehicle operating condition, such as by shifting toward a ratio that permits the motor to operate in a more efficient speed region.

The controller may determine the motor current command as a function of the requested drive output, the measured or estimated transmission speed ratio, and a battery-voltage-based current limit. The controller may determine the CVT ratio command as a function of a target motor speed, a desired wheel torque, a current transmission ratio, and the same or a related battery-voltage-based limit.

In some embodiments, the controller applies rate limits to changes in motor current and CVT ratio to reduce driveline shock. The controller may coordinate the rate of motor current reduction with the rate of CVT ratio change such that vehicle acceleration changes smoothly. For example, if battery voltage sag is detected during a high-throttle event, the controller may reduce motor current gradually while commanding the CVT to a ratio that maintains motor speed in an efficient operating range.

### Example Control Logic

In one embodiment, the controller performs the following operations:

1. receives a battery voltage value;
2. receives a throttle position value;
3. determines or receives a transmission speed ratio;
4. determines a requested motor torque or current based on throttle position;
5. determines a maximum allowable motor current based on battery voltage;
6. compares the requested motor current with the maximum allowable motor current;
7. commands a motor current equal to the lesser of the requested motor current and the maximum allowable motor current;
8. determines a target CVT ratio based on throttle position, battery voltage, and transmission speed ratio; and
9. commands a CVT actuator to adjust the continuously variable transmission toward the target CVT ratio.

The maximum allowable motor current may be determined according to a lookup table, mathematical function, adaptive model, or rule-based control strategy. The target CVT ratio may likewise be determined according to a lookup table, efficiency map, motor speed target, wheel torque target, or optimization routine.

### Battery Voltage-Based Derating

The controller may implement a battery-voltage derating function. For example, when the battery voltage is greater than or equal to a nominal voltage threshold, the controller may permit a maximum motor current corresponding to a full-performance operating mode. When the battery voltage is less than the nominal voltage threshold but greater than a minimum voltage threshold, the controller may reduce the maximum motor current according to a linear, nonlinear, stepped, filtered, or time-dependent function. When the battery voltage is less than the minimum voltage threshold, the controller may limit propulsion torque to a limp-home mode or disable further discharge.

The controller may filter the battery voltage signal to distinguish transient voltage sag from sustained low-voltage conditions. In some embodiments, a first current limit may be based on an instantaneous voltage measurement, while a second current limit may be based on a time-averaged voltage measurement. The commanded motor current may be constrained by the lower of the first and second current limits.

### CVT Ratio Coordination

The transmission speed ratio may be used to determine whether the current CVT ratio is suitable for the requested drive output. If the throttle position indicates a high torque request and the battery voltage is within a normal range, the controller may command a lower effective ratio, providing increased wheel torque. If the battery voltage is low, the controller may avoid commanding a ratio that would require excessive motor current and may instead command a ratio selected to reduce electrical loading.

The controller may determine a target motor speed associated with efficient motor operation. Based on the transmission output speed and the target motor speed, the controller may determine a target transmission ratio. The target motor speed may vary with throttle position and battery voltage. For example, at high throttle and high battery voltage, the target motor speed may be selected for high power output, while at low battery voltage the target motor speed may be selected for reduced current draw or improved efficiency.

---

## Example Independent System Claim

1. **An electric vehicle drivetrain control system comprising:**

   a battery pack;

   an electric traction motor electrically coupled to the battery pack through a motor drive;

   a continuously variable transmission mechanically coupled to the electric traction motor and configured to transmit torque from the electric traction motor to at least one driven wheel;

   a battery voltage sensor configured to generate a battery voltage signal representative of a voltage of the battery pack;

   a throttle position sensor configured to generate a throttle position signal representative of an operator drive request;

   at least one transmission sensor configured to generate a signal representative of a transmission speed ratio of the continuously variable transmission; and

   a controller communicatively coupled to the motor drive and to an actuator of the continuously variable transmission,

   wherein the controller is configured to:
   
   determine a requested motor current based at least in part on the throttle position signal;
   
   determine a maximum allowable motor current based at least in part on the battery voltage signal;
   
   generate a motor current command based on the requested motor current and the maximum allowable motor current;
   
   determine a target transmission ratio based at least in part on the battery voltage signal, the throttle position signal, and the transmission speed ratio; and
   
   command the actuator of the continuously variable transmission to adjust the continuously variable transmission toward the target transmission ratio.

---

## Example Independent Method Claim

2. **A method of controlling an electric vehicle drivetrain having an electric traction motor and a continuously variable transmission, the method comprising:**

   receiving, by a controller, a battery voltage signal representative of voltage of a battery pack;

   receiving, by the controller, a throttle position signal representative of an operator drive request;

   receiving, by the controller, a transmission speed ratio signal representative of a speed ratio of the continuously variable transmission;

   determining, by the controller, a requested motor current based at least in part on the throttle position signal;

   determining, by the controller, a current limit based at least in part on the battery voltage signal;

   commanding, by the controller, motor current to the electric traction motor based on the requested motor current constrained by the current limit; and

   commanding, by the controller, a ratio of the continuously variable transmission based at least in part on the battery voltage signal, the throttle position signal, and the transmission speed ratio.

---

## Example Independent Computer-Readable Medium Claim

3. **A non-transitory computer-readable medium storing instructions that, when executed by one or more processors of an electric vehicle controller, cause the one or more processors to:**

   receive a battery voltage value associated with a battery pack;

   receive a throttle position value associated with an operator drive request;

   receive a transmission speed ratio value associated with a continuously variable transmission;

   determine a requested motor current based on the throttle position value;

   determine a battery-voltage-based current limit based on the battery voltage value;

   generate a motor current command as a function of the requested motor current and the battery-voltage-based current limit; and

   generate a continuously variable transmission ratio command as a function of the battery voltage value, the throttle position value, and the transmission speed ratio value.

---

## Example Dependent Claims

4. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to reduce the maximum allowable motor current when the battery voltage signal indicates that the voltage of the battery pack is below a first voltage threshold.

5. The system of claim 4, wherein the controller is configured to reduce the maximum allowable motor current according to a derating function between the first voltage threshold and a second voltage threshold lower than the first voltage threshold.

6. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to determine the target transmission ratio to maintain a speed of the electric traction motor within a target motor speed range.

7. The system of claim 6, wherein the target motor speed range is selected based at least in part on the battery voltage signal.

8. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to determine the transmission speed ratio based on a motor speed signal and a transmission output speed signal.

9. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to apply a rate limit to changes in the motor current command.

10. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to apply a rate limit to changes in the target transmission ratio.

11. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to coordinate a decrease in the motor current command with a change in the target transmission ratio in response to a decrease in battery voltage.

12. The system of claim 1, wherein the maximum allowable motor current is determined using a lookup table indexed by at least battery voltage.

13. The system of claim 1, wherein the target transmission ratio is determined using a lookup table indexed by battery voltage, throttle position, and transmission speed ratio.

14. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to filter the battery voltage signal before determining the maximum allowable motor current.

15. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to enter a reduced-propulsion mode when the battery voltage signal is below a minimum voltage threshold.

16. The system of claim 1, wherein the controller is configured to increase a requested wheel torque in response to an increase in the throttle position signal and to satisfy the requested wheel torque by jointly selecting the motor current command and the target transmission ratio.

17. The system of claim 1, wherein the continuously variable transmission comprises a belt-and-pulley continuously variable transmission having an electronically controlled actuator.

18. The system of claim 1, wherein the motor drive comprises an inverter configured to regulate phase current supplied to the electric traction motor in response to the motor current command.

19. The method of claim 2, further comprising determining a target motor speed based at least in part on the battery voltage signal and determining the ratio of the continuously variable transmission based on the target motor speed.

20. The method of claim 2, further comprising limiting a rate of change of the commanded motor current and limiting a rate of change of the commanded ratio of the continuously variable transmission to reduce driveline shock.

---

## Additional Embodiment Language

In some embodiments, the controller may prioritize battery protection over driver-requested acceleration. For instance, when the throttle position signal indicates a high operator drive request and the battery voltage signal indicates a low battery voltage condition, the controller may cap the motor current command below the requested motor current and may select a CVT ratio that reduces electrical loading of the battery pack while maintaining vehicle motion.

In other embodiments, the controller may prioritize responsiveness when the battery voltage is within a nominal range. The controller may command increased motor current and a torque-multiplying CVT ratio during launch or acceleration. As vehicle speed increases, the controller may progressively adjust the CVT ratio to reduce motor speed or to maintain the motor near a desired power band.

The controller may store one or more maps correlating battery voltage, throttle position, transmission speed ratio, motor speed, vehicle speed, and desired current. The maps may be calibrated for a particular motor, battery chemistry, vehicle mass, CVT configuration, or desired operating characteristic. The maps may be updated during operation based on measured battery resistance, battery temperature, motor temperature, inverter temperature, or state of charge.

In some embodiments, the controller may calculate a predicted voltage sag based on a proposed motor current command and may select the motor current command and target transmission ratio to prevent the predicted battery voltage from falling below a threshold. The predicted voltage sag may be determined from an estimated internal resistance of the battery pack and a requested current level.

---

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an electric vehicle powertrain invention where a controller simultaneously adjusts drive motor power and CVT speed ratio to improve vehicle range and subsystem efficiency.
counterfactuals.output:
An electric vehicle powertrain invention includes an electric traction motor, a continuously variable transmission (CVT), an energy storage system, and an electronic controller configured to coordinate both motor output and transmission ratio to improve driving range and efficiency.

The controller receives vehicle operating data such as driver torque demand, vehicle speed, battery state of charge, motor speed, motor torque, CVT input/output speeds, temperature, and predicted road load. Rather than controlling the motor and CVT independently, the controller determines a combined operating point for the powertrain. It simultaneously commands:

1. **Drive motor power adjustment**  
   The controller regulates motor torque, motor speed, and electrical power draw from the battery so the motor operates closer to a high-efficiency region of its efficiency map.

2. **CVT speed-ratio adjustment**  
   The controller changes the CVT ratio to alter the relationship between motor speed and wheel speed, allowing the motor to remain in an efficient operating range over a wider range of vehicle speeds and load conditions.

During acceleration, cruising, hill climbing, and regenerative braking, the controller selects a motor power level and CVT ratio that jointly minimize energy consumption while still satisfying requested vehicle performance. For example, during steady cruising, the CVT may be adjusted to keep the motor at a lower-loss speed while the controller reduces unnecessary motor power. During higher load conditions, the controller may shift the CVT ratio to allow the motor to produce required wheel torque without operating in an inefficient high-current region.

The invention may use stored efficiency maps for the motor, inverter, battery, and CVT. The controller evaluates possible motor-power/CVT-ratio combinations and selects an operating point that optimizes total subsystem efficiency rather than only motor efficiency. In some embodiments, the controller also accounts for battery losses, CVT mechanical losses, thermal limits, and anticipated route conditions.

By coordinating drive motor power and CVT speed ratio in real time, the system reduces battery energy consumption, improves motor and inverter efficiency, lowers thermal stress, and increases vehicle driving range compared with electric vehicles using fixed-ratio gearing or independently controlled motor and transmission systems.

counterfactuals.output:
## Technical Summary

An electric vehicle (EV) is provided having an electric traction drive system operatively coupled to a continuously variable transmission (CVT) and configured to operate in a plurality of selectable or automatically selectable driving modes, including an economy mode for optimizing vehicle range.

In one embodiment, the vehicle includes an electric traction motor powered by an onboard energy storage system, such as a rechargeable battery pack. The traction motor is coupled to one or more driven wheels through a continuously variable transmission configured to provide a variable transmission ratio between a motor output shaft and a vehicle drive axle. The CVT may include a belt-and-pulley mechanism, toroidal variator, traction-drive arrangement, e-CVT configuration, or other continuously adjustable ratio mechanism. A vehicle controller is configured to regulate motor torque, regenerative braking, CVT ratio, battery power delivery, and auxiliary power consumption according to a selected operating mode.

The vehicle includes multiple operating modes, such as a normal mode, a performance mode, a traction mode, a towing or load mode, and an economy mode. Each mode may define one or more control maps for motor torque output, accelerator pedal response, CVT ratio scheduling, regenerative braking level, thermal management, and battery discharge limits. The controller may select a mode in response to driver input, navigation data, battery state of charge, predicted route conditions, road grade, traffic conditions, vehicle load, ambient temperature, or a combination thereof.

In the economy mode, the controller operates the electric motor and CVT to increase driving range by maintaining the motor within a high-efficiency operating region. The controller may continuously adjust the CVT ratio to reduce motor speed or motor torque demand where appropriate, minimize electrical losses, reduce peak current draw, and smooth transient power requests. Economy mode may further limit maximum acceleration, reduce available peak torque, increase regenerative braking recovery, optimize coast-down behavior, moderate climate-control loads, and adjust battery thermal management to reduce auxiliary consumption while maintaining component operating limits.

The CVT allows the controller to decouple vehicle speed from motor speed over a broader operating range than a fixed-ratio driveline. Accordingly, during low-load cruising, the CVT may select a ratio that permits the motor to operate at a reduced-loss speed and torque point. During acceleration or grade climbing, the CVT may adjust ratio to provide sufficient wheel torque while avoiding inefficient high-current motor operation. During regenerative braking, the CVT ratio may be adjusted to maintain the motor-generator within an efficient regeneration region, thereby increasing recovered energy.

The control system may include sensors for vehicle speed, motor speed, motor torque, battery state of charge, battery temperature, motor temperature, inverter temperature, accelerator position, brake position, road grade, wheel slip, and transmission ratio. Based on sensor inputs and stored efficiency maps for the motor, inverter, battery, and CVT, the controller determines a target operating point and commands both motor output and transmission ratio. The controller may calculate an energy cost function and select a CVT ratio and torque command that minimize energy consumption while satisfying driver demand and drivability constraints.

In certain embodiments, the economy mode includes predictive energy management. The controller may receive route information from a navigation system and determine upcoming speed limits, elevation changes, traffic congestion, charging locations, and destination distance. The controller may then adjust CVT ratio strategy, torque limits, regenerative braking levels, and accessory loads to preserve battery state of charge and maximize the probability of reaching a destination or charging station.

The system may also provide driver feedback, including estimated range, efficiency score, recommended speed, recommended acceleration behavior, and mode-specific energy savings. The vehicle may automatically prompt the driver to enter economy mode when battery state of charge falls below a threshold or when predicted remaining range is insufficient for a planned route.

The described EV with CVT and multi-mode control provides improved adaptability across driving conditions. In particular, the economy mode coordinates motor operation, transmission ratio selection, regenerative braking, and vehicle energy management to reduce energy consumption and optimize driving range while maintaining acceptable drivability and component protection.
